<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and the clash genuinely narrowed to the "month oil doubles" comparison. CON landed several sharp, original blows: the villager is touched by subsidies through transport and food prices, near-universal cash drifts from "targeted," transfers funded by savings cannot fully precede the price hike, and organized fuel-dependent coalitions defend subsidies more effectively than diffuse deposit recipients. PRO never squarely answered the pass-through or fiscal-sequencing points. But PRO held the decisive frame: CON conceded the subsidy is inefficient and overpays the rich, then answered the pressure question by admitting the finance minister simply borrows, unvoted, while the health budget stays cut. PRO turned that into the cleanest weighing of the debate (design failure that cannot reach a non-fuel-burner vs implementation failures that ministers can be blamed for and fix), and CON never addressed leakage/smuggling or shortages at all. CON's "fails expensively vs fails silently on the poor" was memorable, but rested on assuming perpetual state incapacity while asking the same incapable state to keep borrowing indefinitely. Four clipped CON turns were a minor execution cost. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 forcing CON to say "the minister borrows" [B4.1], then PRO's closing turning that into "a loan taken out without a vote so the SUV's discount can double while the minibus rider's protection doubles on nothing." CON's best counter—the fixed transfer needs a crisis-month vote and "we know how that vote goes"—was strong, but reframing the vote as the first moment of accountability blunted it.</best_rebuttal>
